draft.title: The pigeonhole principle
card: If more than n items are placed into n boxes, at least one box holds two or more items. This is the pigeonhole principle.
To use it, decide what the items are and what the boxes are. The boxes are the possible categories each item can fall into.
Example: 13 people are in a room. There are 12 months, so at least two people share a birth month.
The principle says some box holds at least two. It does not say which box, and it does not say that every box is used.
draft.remember: More items than boxes means some box holds at least two.

a.q: A school has 40 students in a Year 11 class. What is the most that can be guaranteed using the pigeonhole principle about their birth months?
opts: At least two share a birth month
At least four share a birth month
Every month has at least one student
Exactly two share a birth month
a.why: There are 40 items and 12 boxes, so 40 is more than 12 and some month holds at least two students. The principle does not guarantee that every month is used, and it does not say exactly two.
a.clue: Items are students, boxes are months. Is there a box that must be shared?

b.q: Priya has a drawer with loose socks in 4 colours, and she picks socks in the dark. What is the smallest number of socks she must pick to be sure of a matching pair?
b.why: The boxes are the 4 colours. With 4 socks she could have one of each colour, so no pair is certain. A fifth sock must repeat a colour, so 5 is the smallest number that guarantees a pair.
b.clue: Imagine the worst luck: one sock of each colour first.

a.best: At least four share a birth month
also_right: At least two share a birth month

problems.detail: The question asks for the most that can be guaranteed. With 40 students and 12 months, ceil(40/12) = 4, so at least four must share a birth month. The intended answer 'At least two share a birth month' is true but is not the most that can be guaranteed. The why wrongly treats it as the best answer, and the option 'At least four share a birth month' is in fact the correct one.

Getting the 'most guaranteed' answer needs the generalised pigeonhole principle (some box holds at least ceil(n/k) items). The card teaches only the 'at least two' version, so the question goes beyond the card. Either reword it to ask what is guaranteed using the principle as stated, and remove the 'at least four' option, or teach the generalised form.
